title: Effect of Antihypertensive Medication Reduction vs Usual Care on Short-term Blood Pressure Control in Patients With Hypertension Aged 80 Years and Older: The OPTIMISE Randomized Clinical Trial
authors: Sheppard JP, Burt J, Lown M, Temple E, Lowe R, Fraser R, et al.; OPTIMISE Investigators
population: Patients aged 80 years or older at 69 primary care sites in England, with systolic pressure below 150 mm Hg on at least 2 antihypertensive drugs, judged by their physician appropriate for medication reduction; mean age 84.8 years, 48.5% women
funder: This work received joint funding from NIHR CLAHRC at Oxford Health NHS Foundation Trust (P2-501) and the NIHR School for Primary Care Research (335). Drs Sheppard and McManus were funded by an NIHR professorship (NIHR-RP-R2-12-015); further fellowships from the Wellcome Trust/Royal Society and NIHR. The University of Oxford had no role in the design and conduct of the study; collection, management, analysis, and interpretation of the data; preparation, review, or approval of the manuscript; and decision to submit the manuscript for publication.
authorConflicts: Mant reported personal fees from BMS-Pfizer; McManus reported non-financial support from Omron (blood-pressure monitors); other disclosures are NIHR grants.
result: Unblinded non-inferiority trial: removal of one antihypertensive drug (n=282) against usual care (n=287). Systolic pressure below 150 mm Hg at 12 weeks in 229 (86.4%) against 236 (87.7%), adjusted relative risk 0.98 (97.5% one-sided CI 0.92 to infinity), meeting the non-inferiority margin of 0.90. Medication reduction was sustained in 187 (66.3%). Mean systolic pressure rose 3.4 mm Hg (95% CI 1.1 to 5.8) more than with usual care. At least one serious adverse event in 12 (4.3%) against 7 (2.4%), adjusted relative risk 1.72 (0.7 to 4.3). The authors call for research on long-term clinical outcomes.
